The air in Mr. Henderson’s storage unit tasted like dust and forgotten things. Lena wrinkled her nose, pushing a stray strand of auburn hair behind her ear. It was a sweltering August afternoon, and the small, windowless room amplified the heat tenfold. Boxes teetered precariously, draped in cobwebs thick enough to be mistaken for macramé. Discarded furniture huddled in the shadows, and a vague, unsettling aroma—a blend of mothballs, old paper, and something indefinably sweet—hung heavy in the air.

Mr. Henderson, a man perpetually wringing his hands and radiating nervous energy, wrung them even harder. "I just...I just don't know where to start," he mumbled, gesturing vaguely at the chaotic landscape. He was a new neighbor, moved in just a few months ago. A quiet, unassuming man with kind eyes and a perpetually apologetic demeanor. Lena hadn't known him well, but he seemed harmless enough, the type to offer freshly baked cookies and wave politely from his porch.

Lena, on the other hand, was a creature of order. A librarian by trade, she felt a visceral need to categorize and arrange. The sight of this disarray was almost physically painful. "Don't worry," she said with a reassuring smile, hoping to project an air of competence she didn't entirely feel. "We'll tackle it together. Let’s just start by sorting everything into categories. Obvious things first – keep, donate, trash." 

She grabbed a roll of packing tape and a stack of cardboard boxes from the corner, already formulating a plan in her head. A system. A logic to the madness. First, tackle the smaller items, the loose papers and knick-knacks. Then move onto the boxes, assessing their contents without completely unpacking them. Finally, the furniture – the biggest challenge of all. 

Mr. Henderson seemed to visibly deflate with relief. “You’re a lifesaver, Lena. Truly. My late wife, Martha, she… she kept everything. Precious memories, she called them. I just haven’t had the strength to go through it all myself.” He trailed off, his gaze drifting to a faded photograph tucked into the corner of a dusty picture frame. 

Lena, ever pragmatic, didn’t press him. Some things were best left undisturbed, at least for now. She pointed to a pile of old newspapers. “Let’s start there. We can decide whether they're worth keeping or if they go straight to the recycling.”

He nodded, a flicker of something—grief, perhaps?—crossing his face. Together, they began to sift through the layers of forgotten history, the silence broken only by the rustling of paper and the occasional sigh from Mr. Henderson. The afternoon stretched on, the dust motes dancing in the single shaft of sunlight filtering in from the doorway.
